Summary: American missionary and author (1926-2015) who served among the Huaorani people of Ecuador after her husband Jim Elliot was killed there in 1956, and who later lived and worked among them.
Contribution: After her husband's death she carried his missionary story to the world through writing and speaking, and her books on suffering, obedience, and singleness shaped evangelical thinking on Christian womanhood and endurance.
Testimony: She wrote that obedience to God, even through grief, is the ground of Christian peace.

Name: Francis Schaeffer
Summary: American Presbyterian pastor and philosopher (1912-1984) who, with his wife Edith, opened L'Abri as a place where doubters and seekers could ask honest questions.
Contribution: He founded L'Abri Fellowship in Switzerland and argued that Christianity answers the whole of life, influencing evangelical engagement with art, culture, philosophy, and apologetics.

Name: John Stott
Summary: English Anglican clergyman (1921-2011) known for clear biblical preaching and for leadership in global evangelicalism.
Contribution: As rector of All Souls, London, and a leader of the Lausanne movement, he shaped evangelical preaching, biblical exposition, and world mission, and his books remain standard introductions to Christian faith.

Name: Gladys Aylward
Summary: English missionary (1902-1970) who travelled alone to China, worked in Shanxi province, and later cared for orphans in Taiwan.
Contribution: As a missionary in inland China she led children to safety during the Japanese invasion, an act of courage that made her one of the best-known women missionaries of the twentieth century.

Name: Martin Luther King Jr.
Summary: American Baptist minister and civil rights leader (1929-1968) who led the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and was assassinated in Memphis.
Contribution: As a Baptist minister he led the American civil rights movement with nonviolent, biblically grounded appeals to justice, and his preaching joined Christian faith to the dignity of every person.
Testimony: He rooted nonviolent resistance in Christian love of neighbour and enemy alike.

Name: Oscar Romero
Summary: Salvadoran Catholic archbishop (1917-1980) who was assassinated while celebrating Mass after denouncing repression in El Salvador, and who was later canonized.
Contribution: As Archbishop of San Salvador he spoke out for the poor and against state violence, and his preaching and pastoral courage made him a martyr and a symbol of a church standing with the oppressed.

Name: Watchman Nee
Summary: Chinese Christian leader (1903-1972) who preached and wrote across China and was imprisoned for twenty years under the Communist government, dying in prison.
Contribution: He founded the Little Flock movement in China, wrote on the deeper Christian life, and remained faithful through long imprisonment, influencing house churches in China and Christians worldwide.

Name: John Sung
Summary: Chinese evangelist (1901-1944) whose fiery preaching drew large crowds and founded many independent Chinese churches.
Contribution: His evangelistic campaigns helped spark revival across China and Southeast Asia, and his example shaped Chinese evangelical preaching for generations.

Name: Sadhu Sundar Singh
Summary: Indian Christian sadhu (1889-1929) who, after converting from Sikhism, travelled as a barefoot evangelist wearing a saffron robe.
Contribution: As a wandering evangelist in India and beyond he preached a simple gospel of Christ, lived in voluntary poverty, and became a bridge figure between Indian culture and Christian faith.

Name: Toyohiko Kagawa
Summary: Japanese Christian reformer (1888-1960) who lived among the poor in Kobe and became a leading voice for Christian social action in Japan.
Contribution: He combined evangelism with social reform in Japan, founding cooperatives, labour and peace movements, and Christian social institutions that linked faith to the common good.

Name: Eric Liddell
Summary: Scottish Olympic sprinter and missionary (1902-1945) who refused to run on a Sunday at the 1924 Paris Olympics and later served in China.
Contribution: After winning Olympic gold he served as a missionary teacher in China, where he died in an internment camp during the Second World War, becoming a lasting example of faith put before fame.

Name: Jim Elliot
Summary: American missionary (1927-1956) killed, with four colleagues, on the Curaray River in Ecuador during Operation Auca.
Contribution: He was one of five missionaries killed in 1956 while seeking to reach the Huaorani people of Ecuador; his death, and his journal writings, inspired a generation of missionaries.
Testimony: He is remembered for the conviction that no sacrifice for Christ is wasted.

Name: Brother Andrew
Summary: Dutch missionary (1928-2022), born Anne van der Bijl, who began taking Bibles behind the Iron Curtain in the 1950s.
Contribution: He founded Open Doors to smuggle Bibles into Communist countries and support persecuted Christians, giving the suffering church a sustained voice in the West.

Name: Richard Wurmbrand
Summary: Romanian Lutheran pastor (1909-2001) of Jewish background who was imprisoned and tortured for his faith under both Nazi and Communist regimes.
Contribution: After fourteen years in Romanian prisons he founded The Voice of the Martyrs to support persecuted Christians, and his account of suffering under Communism alerted the West to religious persecution.

Name: Lesslie Newbigin
Summary: British missionary and bishop (1909-1998) who served in India for decades and later wrote on mission in the secular West.
Contribution: As a missionary bishop in India and a leader of the World Council of Churches he shaped modern missiology, arguing that the gospel must be proclaimed afresh in both non-Western and secular Western cultures.
KeyWorks: The Gospel in a Pluralist Society

Name: John Mbiti
Summary: Kenyan Anglican priest and theologian (1931-2019) who taught in East Africa and Switzerland and wrote widely on African religion and theology.
Contribution: His study of African traditional religion gave African theology academic standing and helped African Christians articulate faith in their own cultural terms rather than only in Western ones.

Name: William J. Seymour
Summary: African-American preacher (1870-1922) who led the Azusa Street mission in Los Angeles from 1906.
Contribution: He led the Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles, from which modern Pentecostalism spread worldwide across racial lines, making him a founding figure of the Pentecostal movement.

Name: G. K. Chesterton
Summary: English writer and journalist (1874-1936) who converted to Catholicism and became one of the best-known Christian apologists of his age.
Contribution: Through apologetic works and journalism he defended Christian orthodoxy with wit and imagination, influencing both Catholic converts and ordinary readers for generations.

Name: J. R. R. Tolkien
Summary: English writer and Oxford professor (1892-1973), a devout Catholic whose Middle-earth writings carry a deeply Christian moral vision.
Contribution: His fiction, rooted in Catholic faith, gave the twentieth century its most influential Christian imaginative world, shaping how millions picture good, evil, sacrifice, and hope.

Name: Dorothy L. Sayers
Summary: English writer and theologian (1893-1957) known for the Lord Peter Wimsey novels and for popular expositions of Christian doctrine.
Contribution: Her detective fiction, theological essays, and plays defended orthodox Christian doctrine as intellectually serious, and her work on creativity as imaging God influenced Christian thinking about art and work.

Name: Flannery O'Connor
Summary: American Catholic novelist and short-story writer (1925-1964) who lived most of her life in Georgia and died young of lupus.
Contribution: Her short stories and novels gave American Catholic fiction its sharpest twentieth-century voice, portraying grace breaking into ordinary, flawed lives with unsparing moral clarity.
KeyWorks: A Good Man Is Hard to Find

Name: Reinhold Niebuhr
Summary: American theologian (1892-1971) who taught at Union Theological Seminary in New York and became a leading public theologian.
Contribution: His Christian realism shaped Protestant political ethics, warning against both naive idealism and cynicism, and his thought influenced American public life far beyond the church.

Name: Jürgen Moltmann
Summary: German Reformed theologian (1926-2024) whose experience as a prisoner of war shaped a theology centred on the crucified and risen Christ.
Contribution: His theology of hope gave suffering and political engagement a future-oriented Christian grounding, and he became one of the most influential Protestant theologians of the later twentieth century.

Name: Karl Rahner
Summary: German Jesuit theologian (1904-1984) who taught in Innsbruck and Munich and served as a theological adviser at Vatican II.
Contribution: As a leading Catholic theologian of the twentieth century he helped shape the Second Vatican Council and gave modern Catholic theology its language of grace and the church in the modern world.

Name: J. I. Packer
Summary: English-born Canadian theologian (1926-2020) who taught at Regent College, Vancouver, and wrote widely for ordinary readers as well as scholars.
Contribution: His book Knowing God became a classic introduction to Reformed evangelical theology, and his teaching on Scripture, the Puritans, and the Christian life shaped evangelical churches worldwide.

Name: R. C. Sproul
Summary: American Reformed theologian and pastor (1939-2017) who founded Ligonier Ministries and taught at Reformed Theological Seminary.
Contribution: Through Ligonier Ministries, teaching, and writing on the holiness of God he renewed Reformed theology for a popular audience and trained a generation of pastors.

Name: Tim Keller
Summary: American pastor and author (1950-2023) who founded Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan in 1989.
Contribution: As pastor of Redeemer Presbyterian Church in New York he modelled urban, culturally engaged evangelical ministry, and his apologetic writing reached sceptical city readers in large numbers.

Name: Martyn Lloyd-Jones
Summary: Welsh preacher and physician (1899-1981) who ministered at Westminster Chapel in London for three decades.
Contribution: His long ministry at Westminster Chapel, London, and his expository preaching, especially on the Sermon on the Mount, shaped evangelical preaching across Britain and beyond.
KeyWorks: Studies in the Sermon on the Mount

Name: Thomas Merton
Summary: American Trappist monk and writer (1915-1968) who entered the Abbey of Gethsemani in Kentucky after converting to Catholicism.
Contribution: His autobiography and spiritual writings made monastic life and contemplative prayer accessible to modern readers, and he became a leading voice for Christian engagement with other faiths and with social justice.

Name: Henri Nouwen
Summary: Dutch Catholic priest and writer (1932-1996) who taught at Yale, Harvard, and Notre Dame before joining the L'Arche community in Canada.
Contribution: His many books on the spiritual life, written from his own experience of loneliness and belonging, made him one of the most widely read spiritual writers of the later twentieth century.
KeyWorks: The Return of the Prodigal Son

Name: Dorothy Day
Summary: American journalist and social activist (1897-1980) who converted to Catholicism and co-founded the Catholic Worker newspaper and houses of hospitality.
Contribution: She founded the Catholic Worker movement, combining houses of hospitality for the poor with pacifist witness and journalism, and her example shaped Catholic social action in America.

Name: Pope John XXIII
Summary: Italian pope (1881-1963), born Angelo Roncalli, who led the Catholic Church from 1958 until his death and was later canonized.
Contribution: He convened the Second Vatican Council, opening the Catholic Church to renewal, ecumenism, and engagement with the modern world, a turning point for twentieth-century Catholicism.

Name: Pope John Paul II
Summary: Polish pope (1920-2005), born Karol Wojtyła, who led the Catholic Church from 1978 to 2005 and was later canonized.
Contribution: His long pontificate carried out Vatican II, opposed Communism in Eastern Europe, travelled worldwide more than any previous pope, and made him a global moral voice for human dignity.

Name: Pope Benedict XVI
Summary: German pope (1927-2022), born Joseph Ratzinger, who led the Catholic Church from 2005 until his resignation in 2013.
Contribution: As a theologian-pope he gave the church a deeply biblical and Augustinian teaching voice, and his resignation in 2013, the first in centuries, reshaped modern expectations of the papacy.

Name: Edith Stein
Summary: German Jewish-born philosopher (1891-1942) who converted to Catholicism, became a Carmelite nun, and died at Auschwitz; she was later canonized.
Contribution: As a philosopher, Carmelite nun, and martyr at Auschwitz she joined rigorous thought to Christian faith and witness, becoming a symbol of faith under totalitarian persecution.

Name: Maximilian Kolbe
Summary: Polish Franciscan friar (1894-1941) who died at Auschwitz after offering his life for another prisoner, and who was later canonized.
Contribution: He volunteered to take the place of a fellow prisoner condemned to starve at Auschwitz, and his self-sacrifice became one of the most famous Christian martyrdoms of the Second World War.

Name: Luis Palau
Summary: Argentine-born evangelist (1934-2021) who moved to the United States and led large evangelistic festivals across the Spanish-speaking world.
Contribution: As an evangelist to the Spanish-speaking world he preached to millions across Latin America and the United States and founded a ministry that trained Hispanic evangelists.

Name: Reinhard Bonnke
Summary: German Pentecostal evangelist (1940-2019) who founded Christ for All Nations and held mass crusades across Africa for decades.
Contribution: His gospel crusades across Africa drew millions and helped shape African Pentecostal evangelism, making him one of the most influential evangelists on the continent.

Name: Alexander Schmemann
Summary: Russian-born Orthodox priest and theologian (1921-1983) who taught at St Vladimir's Seminary in New York and became dean there.
Contribution: His theology of liturgy and of the world as sacrament renewed Orthodox understanding of worship and mission, and his writings are now standard Orthodox introductions.
KeyWorks: For the Life of the World

Name: Helen Roseveare
Summary: English missionary doctor (1925-2016) who served with the Worldwide Evangelization Crusade in Congo, surviving capture and assault during the Simba rebellion.
Contribution: As a medical missionary in Congo she served through war and hardship, wrote honestly about suffering and God's faithfulness, and became a model of endurance for later missionaries.

Name: Janani Luwum
Summary: Ugandan Anglican archbishop (1922-1977) who was murdered after protesting the violence of the Amin regime and is commemorated in Westminster Abbey.
Contribution: As Archbishop of Uganda he opposed the regime of Idi Amin at the cost of his life, becoming one of the most honoured African martyrs of the twentieth century.
